headline: Bubble Curtains Stop 86% of River Plastic Before It Reaches the Ocean
meta_description: Dutch company's bubble curtain technology captures most floating plastic in rivers, preventing it from reaching oceans. Already operating in Netherlands and Po…
summary_short: A perforated tube and air pump create a rising bubble curtain that intercepts 86% of surface plastic in rivers—stopping pollution before it reaches the sea.
body:
A Dutch company called the Great Bubble Barrier has deployed a deceptively simple technology that stops plastic in its tracks: a perforated tube laid across a river bed, connected to an air pump, that creates a rising curtain of bubbles. When installed diagonally across the waterway, the current naturally carries floating plastic to a collection point on the bank. Universities and independent research institutes have validated the system's effectiveness. It captures approximately 86 percent of surface plastic—a rate that remains stable across deployments. The technology does not block fish or interfere with ship traffic, and it covers the full width and depth of the river.

The barrier currently operates at four locations: Amsterdam, Katwijk, and Harlingen in the Netherlands, and near Vila do Conde in Portugal. Why focus on rivers rather than oceans? Because less than 10 percent of plastic is recycled globally, and the rest enters waterways through poor waste management or accident. By intercepting plastic before it disperses into the open ocean, the Bubble Barrier catches pollution at a stage when intervention is far more effective.

The real work now lies in scaling. The company's ambition is Southeast Asia, where some of the world's most polluted rivers flow. This requires more than engineering expertise. Each deployment demands coordination between governments, local waste managers, and communities. Recognition through Prince William's Earthshot Prize accelerated international efforts significantly. Beyond collection itself, every installation generates crucial data about which types of plastic appear most frequently and where—information that feeds back into policy decisions upstream, helping prevent plastic waste from entering rivers in the first place.
quick_facts: Captures 86% of surface plastic in rivers
Operating in Amsterdam, Katwijk, Harlingen, and Vila do Conde
Perforated tube with air pump creates rising bubble curtain
Does not block fish or ship traffic
